text: Welcome to this overview of machine learning model optimization. I will cover three key areas today: quantization, pruning, and knowledge distillation. Each technique offers different tradeoffs between model size, inference speed, and accuracy. Let us begin with quantization. The core idea is straightforward. Instead of storing model weights as thirty two bit floating point numbers, we can use lower precision formats. The most common approach is INT8 quantization, which reduces memory footprint by four times. Research from Google Brain published in 2022 showed that post-training quantization to INT8 achieves less than one percent accuracy loss on standard benchmarks including ImageNet and GLUE. For more aggressive compression, INT4 quantization is gaining traction. The GPTQ algorithm introduced by Frantar et al can quantize large language models to four bits with minimal perplexity degradation. Specifically, they demonstrated that a 175 billion parameter model quantized to INT4 maintains ninety seven percent of its original performance while requiring only twenty five percent of the memory. The key insight is layer-wise quantization with Hessian-based error correction. Moving on to pruning. Structured pruning removes entire neurons, attention heads, or layers. The lottery ticket hypothesis proposed by Frankle and Carlin suggests that dense networks contain sparse subnetworks that can match full model performance. In practice, magnitude-based pruning at fifty to seventy percent sparsity ratios is reliable across architectures. Unstructured pruning achieves higher compression ratios but requires specialized hardware support. Current generation GPUs cannot efficiently exploit unstructured sparsity. The Ampere architecture introduced two to four structured sparsity support, which is a middle ground. Benchmarks show one point five to two times speedup with minimal accuracy impact. Finally, knowledge distillation transfers knowledge from a large teacher model to a smaller student model. The DistilBERT paper demonstrated that a student model with forty percent fewer parameters can retain ninety seven percent of BERT base performance on GLUE tasks. The training procedure involves minimizing a combined loss. The first term is the standard cross entropy with ground truth labels. The second term is the KL divergence between teacher and student softmax outputs at elevated temperature. Temperature values between four and twenty work well empirically. Recent work on multi-teacher distillation and progressive distillation has further improved results. In summary, these three techniques are complementary. A practical deployment pipeline might first distill, then quantize, and optionally prune. This combination can achieve ten to fifty times model compression with less than five percent accuracy degradation. The choice depends on your hardware constraints, latency requirements, and acceptable quality thresholds. I recommend starting with INT8 quantization as it provides the best effort to reward ratio. Thank you for your attention.
